Seven Videos, Measured

Seven reference explainers on money and policy, 65 minutes in all, downloaded at 480p for analysis only and deleted after. Every hard cut found, every shot length measured, speech rate from the auto-captions, loudness from the soundtrack, and one frame after every cut laid out so the design could be read from stills. Then ours, the same way.

n/m: not measurable. The cut detector reads animated maps (Wendover) and popping type (Half as Interesting) as cuts, so their shot counts are meaningless; their frames are still shown below. "Cuts mid-phrase" is the share of cuts that fall neither inside a speech pause nor within 0.3s after one, measured from the audio. Our own cuts fall on word boundaries by construction, so that column does not apply.

What the numbers say

1.5–3.1s
Their median shot. Ours is 4.6s. The first minute is their fastest (1.0–1.9s median); it is our slowest (4.4s). Our first cut of this video felt too fast to you at a 2.8s median because the shots were random, not because they were short. Theirs are shorter and do not feel random, because each one shows the thing being said.
83–95%
Cuts land mid-phrase. Not on pauses, not on sentence ends. The picture changes when the narration names a new thing, in the middle of the sentence. This is what "cut on the words" means in practice, and it is what the anchors now do. Our first cut scored boundaries by sentence end and silence; that was the wrong instinct.
154–186
Words a minute. Ours: 134 while speaking, 96 once pauses are counted. We are the slowest talker here by a wide margin. The [slowly] directions and the 1.7s section pauses compound it.
5 of 7
Footage is evidence, not illustration. News footage of the actual event (PolyMatter, Search Party), documents and headlines on screen with a highlighter (Vox, Johnny Harris), a real stat card with its source (WSJ). Stock B-roll of a generic hand is the minority everywhere. This is the gap our stock-only pipeline cannot close with better search.
7 of 7
A persistent frame. A corner mark (WSJ, Vox), a colour system (Search Party green and black, Vox teal grid, Wendover grey-blue), dated lower-thirds and name labels. Two hundred cuts read as one film because the frame never changes. Ours has a palette and a card family but no mark and no lower-thirds.
−16 to −21
LUFS. None of them sits at YouTube's −14 reference. Ours at −15.5 is the loudest of the set. Stop chasing −14.

What changes in our pipeline

  1. Documents become a shot kind. For a policy channel the documents are the footage: the Mint's annual report page with the 3.69¢ line, the Treasury memo, the bill on congress.gov, the press headlines. US government documents are public domain; headlines are short quotation. Render the real page with Playwright, push in, sweep a highlighter over the quoted line on the word. This is the Vox and Harris device, and it needs no stock search at all.
  2. Pace like PolyMatter, not like Harris. Target a 2.5–3s median with 1.8–2.2s in the first minute, and only through anchors: every shorter shot must be the named thing. Lower the section-end weight in the boundary scorer; the trade cuts mid-sentence on the noun.
  3. Talk at 150+. Keep [slowly] on two lines, not five. Section pause 1.7s to 1.0s. Re-measure after the next voice pass.
  4. A frame that never leaves. A small mark in one corner, a dated lower-third where a date is spoken, name labels for agencies. The Search Party power diagram that grows across the video is worth copying as a device: one graphic that returns, larger each time.
  5. Faces we cannot have; the faceless two show the compensation. PolyMatter and Wendover carry a video with archive footage, maps and data. Ours are documents, the Polaroid board and the kinetic figures. Lean on those, not on stock people.

The frames

One frame after each detected cut, in order, sampled to 64 when there were more. This is the evidence for the observations under each.

WSJ · Trump Wants to End Penny Production. Here Are the Pros and Cons.

faces + B-roll274k views

Same topic as ours. Two interview heads carry the argument; B-roll of pennies pouring, a coin-counting drawer, the Mint floor. One stat card, white on dark: $85+ MILLION with Source: U.S. Mint under it. Single-word callouts on the footage (SEIGNIORAGE). A small WSJ mark in the corner of every frame.

Vox · Why can't prices just stay the same?

presenter + documents2.5M views

Headlines and reports as footage: screenshots of the IMF, NYT, Forbes with a yellow highlighter over the phrase being read. Charts with a title line and a source line. A teal grid brand ground with dollar icons for the abstract passages. Black-and-white archive for history. A presenter in a chair between them.

PolyMatter · Why India Banned 86% of its Currency

faceless, archive2.1M views

Faceless. Almost every frame is news footage of the actual event: the queues, the notes changing hands, Modi at the podium, the bank doors. Very few graphics. The footage is not illustration, it is evidence. Sponsor block at the end.

Search Party · Why Putin is so hard to overthrow

faceless + interviews3.5M views

A dark green and black system on every frame: dated lower-thirds (June 24, 2023), name labels, a recurring power-structure diagram in green blocks that grows as the argument does. Archive footage with burned-in translation. Two remote interviews. The system makes 200 cuts feel like one film.

Johnny Harris · How Capitalism Changed the Face of War

on camera + props1.6M views

Physical evidence on camera: hands on books, a highlighter dragged across printed text, maps on the wall, archive photographs, screen recordings of his own research. 521 cuts in 21 minutes. Text appears as a printed page, rarely as a graphic.

Wendover · How Airports Make Money

faceless, maps5.2M views

Animated maps with a persistent label (Retail Revenue Per Passenger) while the map moves country to country, airport footage between them, a grey-blue palette throughout. Hard cuts are rare; the picture changes by animation, which the cut detector cannot see.

Half as Interesting · How Australia Printed a Typo 46 Million Times

faceless, kinetic text1.6M views

Bold yellow condensed type with a dark outline popping over footage, one joke per shot, text pages as backgrounds. Kinetic text is the whole grammar here; the detector reads every pop as a cut.

Ours · It Costs More Than One Cent To Make One Cent, third cut

faceless, stock + polaroid

Every shot, in order. Against the set above: coherent palette and card family, no persistent mark, no documents, no footage of the actual subject, and a shot count you can read on one page where theirs need three.

Limits of this study

I see stills, not motion; how an animation feels in time I cannot judge. The cut detector (ffmpeg scdet, threshold 6, calibrated against our own cut list at 22 of 33 recalled) misses dissolves and over-counts kinetic type. Speech rate comes from YouTube's auto-captions, which carry no punctuation, so phrase boundaries had to be taken from the audio. Seven videos is a sample, chosen for topic and for being the channels this channel is compared to, not a survey.
